1025.title: Unit Circle
1025.heading: Unit Circle
1025.content: The unit circle is the circle of radius one centered at the origin. The point reached by an angle $\theta$ has coordinates $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, extending [[Trigonometric Ratios]] beyond acute angles. Its circumference also defines [[Angle Measure in Radians]] and makes the signs and periodicity of sine and cosine geometrically visible.

1028.heading: Unique Selling Point
1028.content:
A unique selling point is a meaningful way a game is attractively distinct from alternatives already familiar to its audience. A concept commonly identifies a small set of these differences rather than claiming novelty in every feature.

The point must matter to the [[Target Audience]] and be visible in the proposed experience, not merely in internal technology. It helps explain why a player or stakeholder should choose this game in a [[Game Concept Document]] or [[Game Pitch]].

1031.title: Unique Factorization of Polynomials
1031.heading: Unique Factorization of Polynomials
1031.content:
Every nonconstant polynomial over a [[Field]] can be expressed as a product of [[Irreducible Polynomial]]s. Any two such factorizations have the same number of factors after reordering and multiplication of factors by nonzero constants.

The theorem extends from one-variable to multivariable polynomial rings. It makes irreducible factors the basic multiplicative building blocks of polynomial equations.

The book derives existence by repeatedly factoring reducible polynomials and uses irreducible divisibility to control uniqueness up to order and associates. This makes irreducible factors the stable data of a polynomial over a field.

1034.title: Union of Sets
1034.heading: Union of Sets
1034.content:
The union of sets contains every element that belongs to at least one of them. Finite unions combine listed collections, while indexed unions combine a family of sets.

A union of substructures need not itself be a substructure unless the family satisfies additional nesting conditions.

For two sets, A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A ∨ x ∈ B}; its definition mirrors logical disjunction and includes elements that occur in either set or both.

1037.title: Unintended Consequence
1037.heading: Unintended Consequence
1037.content:
An unintended consequence is an effect that arises outside the immediate purpose of an action. It often appears when a local fix participates in a larger or delayed [[Feedback Loop]] that was not considered.

A change may reduce a visible problem in the short term while strengthening the conditions that recreate it later. [[Systems Thinking]] helps reveal these effects by widening the boundary and timescale of analysis.

1040.content:
Unguided alternative clustering seeks several distinct high-quality solutions without a user specifying what the alternatives should mean. Diversity penalties or sequential objectives discourage each solution from repeating structures already found.

The approach can reveal hidden views for exploration, but mathematical distinctness does not guarantee domain relevance. Comparing features, prototypes, and stability helps determine whether an alternative is interpretable rather than merely different.

1043.heading: Unequal Group Power Calculation
1043.content:
An unequal group power calculation allows comparison groups to have different sample sizes. One group's size may be fixed by disease prevalence, recruitment limits, or the available records while the calculation solves for the other.

Imbalance generally supplies less information than the same total sample divided evenly. Planning should therefore distinguish the number of available events from the total number of observations and avoid assuming that a large dataset automatically makes every subgroup comparison well powered.

1046.title: Undirected Graph
1046.heading: Undirected Graph
1046.content:
An undirected graph has edges that can be traversed in either direction. An edge connecting vertices $A$ and $B$ therefore represents the same connection whether it is approached from $A$ or from $B$.

Reciprocal social relationships and two-way bridges can be modeled this way. When the direction of a relationship matters, the appropriate model is instead a [[Directed Graph]].

1052.title: Undefined Rational Expression
1052.heading: Undefined Rational Expression
1052.content:
A rational expression is undefined at any value that makes its denominator zero. Before simplifying

$$\frac{x^2-1}{x-1},$$

the value (x=1) must be excluded. Factoring and cancelling gives (x+1), but the original expression still has no value at (x=1).

Restrictions should therefore be identified before cancellation, multiplication, or cross multiplication. A transformation can preserve equality only on the domain where every expression and division used in the step is defined.

1055.heading: Underdetermined Linear System
1055.content:
An underdetermined linear system has fewer equations than unknowns. When consistent, it typically has infinitely many solutions because some variables remain free.

A [[Minimum-Norm Solution]] selects the solution closest to the origin. It can be expressed using a [[Pseudoinverse]] when the needed rank conditions hold.

1058.heading: Underdetermined Least Squares
1058.content:
Underdetermined least squares addresses a consistent system with fewer equations than unknowns by selecting a solution using an additional criterion.

The usual choice is the [[Minimum-Norm Solution]], the solution closest to the origin and orthogonal to the null space. Under full row rank it can be written $A^T(AA^T)^{-1}b$.

1061.title: Uncountable Set
1061.heading: Uncountable Set
1061.content:
An uncountable set cannot be placed in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. Its members cannot all be exhausted by any infinite sequence indexed by natural numbers.

The real numbers are uncountable, and removing a [[Countable Set|countable subset]] from an uncountable set leaves an uncountable remainder. [[Cantor Diagonal Argument]] demonstrates this by constructing an element omitted from every proposed list.

1063.sourceSearchName: uncertain rule based classification uncertain rule based classification
1063.title: Uncertain Rule-Based Classification
1063.heading: Document

1064.sourceSearchName: uncertain rule based classification uncertain rule based classification
1064.title: Uncertain Rule-Based Classification
1064.heading: Uncertain Rule-Based Classification
1064.content:
Uncertain rule-based classification replaces binary rule satisfaction with the probability that an imprecise observation satisfies the antecedent. Coverage and confidence therefore accumulate fractional support.

At prediction time, a rule's influence can be weighted by its satisfaction probability. This distinguishes a case concentrated inside the rule region from one whose possible values only barely overlap it.

1065.sourceSearchName: uncertain rule based classification uncertain rule based classification
1065.title: Uncertain Rule-Based Classification

1067.title: Unclassed Choropleth
1067.heading: Unclassed Choropleth
1067.content: An unclassed choropleth maps each numeric value directly to a position on a continuous color scale. It preserves more of the variable's ordering than a [[Classed Choropleth]] and avoids artificial interval boundaries. However, viewers cannot reliably distinguish many fine color differences or recover exact values. The continuous legend must show the numeric range, and outliers can compress most regions into a narrow visual span.

1070.title: Uncertainty Sampling
1070.heading: Uncertainty Sampling
1070.content:
Uncertainty sampling requests the label of the case for which the current classifier is least certain. Binary models often use proximity to a probability of one half or to the decision boundary, while multiclass models use small margins or high entropy.

The method is simple and directly attacks ambiguous regions, but it may repeatedly choose outliers or an unrepresentative pocket. Combining uncertainty with density or diversity can make the labeling budget cover the data more usefully.

1072.sourceSearchName: uncertainty density function uncertainty density function
1072.title: Uncertainty Density Function
1072.heading: Document

1073.sourceSearchName: uncertainty density function uncertainty density function
1073.title: Uncertainty Density Function
1073.heading: Uncertainty Density Function
1073.content:
An uncertainty density function assigns probabilities to the possible values of an imprecisely observed attribute or object. It preserves more information than a simple interval because likely and unlikely realizations are distinguished.

Classification algorithms can integrate a test, rule, or distance over this density. The result reflects expected behavior across possible values rather than pretending that a single point estimate was observed without error.

1074.sourceSearchName: uncertainty density function uncertainty density function
1074.title: Uncertainty Density Function

1075.title: Uncertain Decision Tree Classification

1076.sourceSearchName: uncertain decision tree classification uncertain decision tree classification
1076.title: Uncertain Decision Tree Classification
1076.heading: Uncertain Decision Tree Classification
1076.content:
Uncertain decision tree classification evaluates how probability mass, rather than a single value, crosses a candidate split. An uncertain observation may contribute fractionally to more than one child node.

Split quality and class distributions are computed from these weighted contributions. Prediction similarly aggregates possible paths, retaining uncertainty through the tree instead of assigning the observation prematurely to one branch.

1079.title: Uncertain Data
1079.heading: Uncertain Data
1079.content:
Uncertain data represents values or item occurrences with alternatives, probabilities, or imprecision rather than assuming every recorded fact is definite. Uncertainty can arise from sensing error, incomplete observation, inference, integration, or noisy sources.

Mining must propagate that uncertainty into support and pattern criteria instead of silently converting probabilistic records into certain ones.

1081.sourceSearchName: uncertain data classification uncertain data classification
1081.title: Uncertain Data Classification
1081.heading: Document

1082.sourceSearchName: uncertain data classification uncertain data classification
1082.title: Uncertain Data Classification
1082.heading: Uncertain Data Classification
1082.content:
Uncertain data classification predicts labels when an attribute is represented by a range, set, or probability distribution rather than one exact value. Measurement error, imputation, privacy transformations, and indirect sensing can all create this representation.

A classifier must aggregate over possible realizations or derive statistics of the uncertainty distribution. Replacing every uncertain value by its mean can discard variation that changes split, distance, density, or likelihood decisions.

1083.title: Uncertain Data Classification

1084.title: Uncertain Associative Classification
1084.heading: Document

1085.sourceSearchName: uncertain associative classification uncertain associative classification
1085.title: Uncertain Associative Classification
1085.heading: Uncertain Associative Classification
1085.content:
Uncertain associative classification mines class association rules when items or attribute conditions have probabilistic presence. Expected support replaces the integer count used with certain transactions.

Rules must remain frequent and class-informative after uncertainty is integrated. Treating every possible item as present exaggerates support, while thresholding probabilities too early discards graded evidence supplied by the uncertainty model.

1086.title: Uncertain Associative Classification

1088.title: Unbounded Interval
1088.heading: Unbounded Interval
1088.content:
An unbounded interval extends indefinitely in at least one direction on the [[Number Line]]. The inequality (x>-1) describes every real number to the right of (-1), while (x\leq2) extends without bound to the left.

An arrow shows the unbounded direction in a graph. The finite endpoint is open for a strict inequality and closed for an inclusive one. Infinity is not a real endpoint that can be included; it indicates that no finite boundary stops the interval.

1091.sourceSearchName: unambiguous computational steps unambiguous computational steps
1091.title: Unambiguous Computational Steps
1091.heading: Unambiguous Computational Steps
1091.content:
A computational step must specify an operation precisely enough that different competent executors obtain the same result. Replacing vague instructions with elementary arithmetic, comparison, and symbol manipulation makes a method reproducible and eventually mechanizable.

Unambiguity is a source of trust, not a guarantee of correctness. The steps can still embody a faulty model or be connected in the wrong order, so the entire procedure and its assumptions must also be examined.

1094.title: Ultrasound
1094.heading: Ultrasound
1094.content: Ultrasound is sound with frequency above the upper range of ordinary human hearing, conventionally above 20 kHz. Its shorter wavelength supports fine spatial resolution, while reflection depends on changes in acoustic impedance between materials. Coupling gel reduces the strong reflection that an air gap would otherwise produce at a transducer boundary.

1097.sourceSearchName: ultrametricity triangle coefficient ultrametricity triangle coefficient
1097.title: Ultrametricity Triangle Coefficient
1097.heading: Ultrametricity Triangle Coefficient
1097.content:
The book measures inherent ultrametricity by examining triples of points before imposing a clustering tree. In a Euclidean embedding, a triple is counted when its triangle is approximately equilateral or isosceles with a small base; the coefficient is the proportion of counted, nondegenerate triples.

Its implementation samples triples when exhaustive enumeration is too costly and uses a chosen angular tolerance, so the value depends on both the embedding and approximation rule. It can compare datasets or encodings for hierarchical tendency without assuming that a particular linkage algorithm's fitted dendrogram is the ground truth.

1100.sourceSearchName: ultrametric mind hypothesis ultrametric mind hypothesis
1100.title: Ultrametric Mind Hypothesis
1100.heading: Ultrametric Mind Hypothesis
1100.content:
The ultrametric mind hypothesis treats nested classes of stimuli or concepts as a possible representation for some unconscious generalization. Inside one cluster, items are equivalent at that resolution; a higher branch groups several such classes into a broader one.

The book connects this structure to Matte Blanco's account of symmetric reasoning and suggests that hierarchical computation could make pattern matching efficient. This is an exploratory analogy and research proposal. Measuring an ultrametric tendency in text does not by itself prove that a particular brain process uses a tree-distance algorithm.

1101.title: Ultrametric Mind Hypothesis
1101.heading: References

1103.title: Ultrametric Inequality
1103.heading: Ultrametric Inequality
1103.content:
An ultrametric is a distance satisfying the strong triangle inequality: the distance from x to z is no greater than the larger of the distances from x to y and y to z. It is more restrictive than the ordinary triangle inequality.

For any three points, the two largest pairwise distances are equal. The corresponding triangle is equilateral or isosceles with a small base. This geometry is why nested cluster relationships can be represented by a rooted tree rather than by arbitrary overlap among neighborhoods.

1105.sourceSearchName: ultrametric distance matrix ultrametric distance matrix
1105.title: Ultrametric Distance Matrix
1105.heading: Document

1106.sourceSearchName: ultrametric distance matrix ultrametric distance matrix
1106.title: Ultrametric Distance Matrix
1106.heading: Ultrametric Distance Matrix
1106.content:
An ultrametric distance matrix records the tree-derived distance for every pair of leaves. Reordering its rows and columns consistently can reveal nested blocks: low within-cluster values collect near the diagonal and higher values separate larger branches.

The book demonstrates this with iris measurements, a Ward dendrogram, and the matrix read from that dendrogram. The matrix is more than a visualization aid: its ordered block structure is a numerical fingerprint of hierarchical relationships and can guide seriation of observations.

1107.sourceSearchName: ultrametric distance matrix ultrametric distance matrix
1107.title: Ultrametric Distance Matrix
1107.heading: References

1108.sourceSearchName: ultrametric ball nesting ultrametric ball nesting
1108.title: Ultrametric Ball Nesting
1108.heading: Document

1109.sourceSearchName: ultrametric ball nesting ultrametric ball nesting
1109.title: Ultrametric Ball Nesting
1109.heading: Ultrametric Ball Nesting
1109.content:
In an ultrametric space, two balls are either disjoint or one is contained in the other; they cannot overlap only partly. Every point of a ball can serve as its center, and balls are both open and closed in the associated topology.

These unusual properties explain the tree picture. At a chosen distance threshold, a ball acts like a cluster node; raising the threshold encloses it in a larger node, while unrelated nodes stay apart. The resulting order is by set inclusion along a branch, not a total order across all branches.

UK-means represents each uncertain object through a probability distribution and assigns it to the center with the smallest expected squared distance. Cluster centers are updated from the expected contributions of their assigned objects.

Using expectation propagates positional uncertainty into the partition rather than replacing each object with one sampled or nominal point. Like ordinary K-means, it favors compact groups and can converge to a local optimum.

1115.title: UDP Multicast
1115.heading: UDP Multicast
1115.content:
UDP multicast sends a datagram to a multicast group address so several subscribed receivers can obtain the same packet. A sender does not establish a separate reliable connection with every recipient.

This supports one-to-many discovery or distribution with low transport overhead. Delivery, ordering, and group membership changes are not guaranteed like a TCP session, so the application must tolerate missing or duplicated messages when those outcomes matter.

1121.title: Ubiquitous Computing
1121.heading: Ubiquitous Computing
1121.content:
Ubiquitous computing is the idea that computing devices, infrastructure, and access to them can be mobile or distributed throughout the physical environment, giving people computational access across places and situations.

Because computation is no longer confined to a desktop, conventional interface components may be unsuitable. A ubiquitous system can use spatial context, embedded devices, and [[Tangible User Interface|tangible interfaces]], and may overlap with [[Augmented Reality]] or other forms of [[3D Interaction]].

Ubiquitous computing can remain calm and operate in the background, or it can expose an interface when interaction is needed. AR supplies one situated interface for that distributed computation by placing information directly in the physical context to which it applies.

Cloud services extend ubiquitous computing by making applications and organizational information available from different locations, devices, and times. This goes beyond [[Bring Your Own Device]] because the central idea is access wherever it is needed, not merely ownership of the client hardware.

1123.title: Ubiquitous Language

1124.title: Ubiquitous Language
1124.heading: Ubiquitous Language
1124.content: A Ubiquitous Language is the precise language shared by domain experts and developers within one context. Its terms and behaviors appear consistently in discussions, models, code, tests, interfaces, and data structures. Ubiquitous does not mean one vocabulary for an entire organization; it means the same vocabulary is used vertically through every artifact inside its boundary. When a word develops incompatible meanings, [[Context-Specific Language]] indicates that the model may be crossing a [[Linguistic Boundary]].

1127.title: TypeScript
1127.heading: TypeScript
1127.content:
TypeScript is a Microsoft-created superset of JavaScript that adds type checking, class and type declarations, and object-oriented language features during development. Its source is transpiled into standard JavaScript that browsers can execute.

Angular uses TypeScript for components, services, modules, and tests. The generated JavaScript can retain a connection to its source through a [[JavaScript Source Map]], allowing client-side debugging at the TypeScript level.

1130.title: TypeScript Access Modifier
1130.heading: TypeScript Access Modifier
1130.content:
A TypeScript access modifier declares how a class member may be used. `public` permits external access, `private` limits access to the class, `protected` permits the class and its descendants, and `readonly` prevents reassignment after initialization.

These constraints are enforced by the TypeScript compiler rather than by the generated JavaScript at runtime. They communicate intended boundaries and help the compiler detect inappropriate use during development.

1133.content:
Caillois's framework describes four recurring forms of play: agon centers on competition, alea on chance, mimicry on role-playing, and ilinx on altered perception or vertigo. A game may combine several rather than belonging exclusively to one.

The framework also places play on a continuum from ludus, which is structured by formal rules, to paidia, which is spontaneous and improvisational. These dimensions help describe the experience more precisely than a broad [[Game Genre]] label alone.

1148.heading: Tyche Storage Protocol
1148.content:
Tyche is the book's Ethernet-based protocol for converged networked storage. It organizes communication channels and storage messages around a lean I/O path intended to use commodity Ethernet efficiently.

Its implementation combines preallocated memory, custom queues, NUMA-aware work placement, adaptive batching, copy reduction, and multiple network interfaces to address small-request latency and multicore scaling.

1208.title: Tutorial Level
1208.heading: Tutorial Level
1208.content:
A tutorial level teaches controls, actions, challenges, and rules through an intentionally arranged early experience. It lets the player learn by doing rather than requiring all instructions to be read in advance.

New demands should be introduced with clear feedback and enough safety to experiment, then recombined to confirm understanding. A tutorial succeeds when later play can rely on what the player learned.

1211.sourceSearchName: turing decidable language turing decidable language
1211.title: Turing-Decidable Language
1211.heading: Turing-Decidable Language
1211.content:
A language is Turing-decidable when a [[Turing Machine]] computes its characteristic function: it halts on every input with 1 for membership and 0 for nonmembership. The requirement to halt in both cases distinguishes decision from mere acceptance.

Turing-decidable languages are also called [[Recursive Language|recursive languages]]. A language is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are [[Turing-Acceptable Language|Turing-acceptable]].

1213.heading: Document

1214.sourceSearchName: turing computable function turing computable function
1214.title: Turing-Computable Function
1214.heading: Turing-Computable Function
1214.content:
A function from strings to strings is Turing-computable when a [[Turing Machine]] halts on every input in its domain with the function's value arranged as its output. The machine must therefore both produce the correct string and halt in a defined output configuration.

Computable functions are closed under composition because one machine can compute the first function and then run a machine for the second on that result. This formalizes effective calculation independently of a particular programming language.

1217.sourceSearchName: turing acceptable language turing acceptable language
1217.title: Turing-Acceptable Language
1217.heading: Turing-Acceptable Language
1217.content:
A language is Turing-acceptable when some [[Turing Machine]] halts exactly on the strings in the language. For a string outside the language, the machine may run forever rather than halt with an explicit rejection.

Every [[Turing-Decidable Language|decidable language]] is acceptable, but the converse fails. Turing-acceptable languages are exactly the [[Recursively Enumerable Language|recursively enumerable languages]] and exactly the languages generated by general grammars.

1220.heading: Turing Universality and Programmability
1220.content:
Alan Turing described a formal machine that could simulate any other rule-governed computation when supplied with an appropriate description. This made programmability, rather than a fixed mechanical purpose, the defining quality of a general computer.

The model used an unbounded symbolic tape and elementary state transitions, not practical hardware. Its importance was to show that one finite mechanism could realize an open-ended range of procedures.

1223.title: Turing Machine
1223.heading: Turing Machine
1223.content:
A Turing machine is an idealized computational machine consisting of an unbounded tape divided into cells, a movable read-write head, a finite set of states, and an instruction table. Each instruction uses the current state and scanned symbol to choose a new state, write a symbol, and move the head one cell left or right.

Its operations are deliberately elementary, yet a properly constructed Turing machine can implement any [[Algorithm]]. This makes it a formal model for reasoning about what computation can accomplish, independent of the speed or physical construction of a particular computer.

Formally, its transition function maps the current non-halting state and scanned symbol to a written symbol, a one-cell left or right move, and a new state. A computation may reach its halt state or continue forever, allowing the model to distinguish [[Turing-Decidable Language|decision]] from [[Turing-Acceptable Language|acceptance]].

1229.title: Turbulent Flow
1229.heading: Turbulent Flow
1229.content: Turbulent flow contains irregular eddies and strong mixing rather than stable parallel streamlines. It develops when inertial effects overwhelm viscous damping above a geometry-dependent critical Reynolds number. Turbulence increases drag and energy loss, so formulas derived for [[Laminar Flow]] cannot generally be carried into the turbulent regime unchanged.

1232.title: Tuning Stage
1232.heading: Tuning Stage
1232.content:
The tuning stage is the final design stage in which the team polishes and balances an already defined game without adding new features. Values, timing, difficulty, presentation, and usability can still change.

Restricting new scope lets implementation, debugging, and testing converge. Tuning is therefore different from elaboration: it adjusts the existing design rather than expanding what the product promises.

1235.title: Tuckman Model
1235.heading: Tuckman Model
1235.content:
The Tuckman model describes team development as forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. Members first orient to the group, encounter conflict, establish workable norms, develop effective coordination, and eventually separate or transform.

The sequence is a diagnostic model rather than a guaranteed linear schedule. Membership or context changes can return a mature team to earlier coordination needs.

1238.title: Truth Table
1238.heading: Truth Table
1238.content:
A truth table lists the value of a [[Compound Propositions|compound proposition]] for every assignment of truth values to its [[Propositional Variable|propositional variables]]. A formula with n distinct variables requires 2^n rows because every variable independently has two possible values.

Truth tables mechanically test whether two formulas are [[Logically Equivalent]] and whether a formula is a [[Tautology]]. Their exhaustive character is reliable for small formulas but becomes impractical as the number of variables grows.

1241.title: Trustworthy AI
1241.heading: Trustworthy AI
1241.content:
Trustworthy AI is the policy goal of building systems whose operation and governance justify reliance. It combines technical qualities such as safety and reliability with ethical and institutional qualities such as fairness, privacy, accountability, respect for autonomy, and intelligibility.

Trust should be earned rather than manufactured through reassuring design or branding. A user may understand a system and reasonably decide not to trust it. Demonstrating trustworthiness therefore requires evidence, [[Algorithmic Auditability]], clear responsibility, and remedies when commitments fail. The aim is not maximum trust, but well-calibrated trust supported by enforceable practices.

1244.title: Truss
1244.heading: Truss
1244.content:
A truss is a load-bearing structure formed from slender members connected at joints idealized as pins. Under this idealization, members transmit axial tension or compression rather than bending moment.

Finite element analysis represents each member with a truss element and enforces equilibrium through shared joint degrees of freedom. Loads and support constraints are applied at the nodes.

1246.sourceSearchName: trust in mobile commerce trust in mobile commerce

1247.sourceSearchName: trust in mobile commerce trust in mobile commerce
1247.title: Trust in Mobile Commerce
1247.heading: Trust in Mobile Commerce
1247.content:
Trust in mobile commerce is a user's willingness to rely on a service when its data practices and future behavior cannot be observed completely. Trust can lower perceived privacy risk and make disclosure more likely.

Trust is not a substitute for governance. A user may trust the visible service while being unaware of advertisers, analytics providers, or brokers that receive the information, so transparent boundaries and enforceable duties remain necessary.

1250.heading: Truss Translational Degree of Freedom
1250.content:
A truss translational degree of freedom is a nodal displacement component along a global coordinate axis. A planar truss node normally has one x translation and one y translation.

Supports prescribe selected components, while connected members couple the remaining components through their oriented stiffness. Consistent ordering of these translations controls assembly of the global matrix.

1253.heading: Truss Support Reaction

A truss support reaction is the force supplied by a restraint to maintain equilibrium. Reactions are associated with prescribed nodal degrees of freedom and are not independent applied loads.

After solving free displacements, reactions are recovered from the original global stiffness relation. Their resultant should balance the externally applied truss loads.

1256.heading: Truss Stiffness Assembly
1256.content:
Truss stiffness assembly superposes the oriented stiffness matrices of all members into one global matrix. Each element contributes to the degrees of freedom of its two endpoint nodes.

Shared-node contributions are added, which couples the member network and enforces joint equilibrium. Boundary conditions then reduce the system to the unknown joint translations.

1259.title: Truss Member
1259.heading: Truss Member
1259.content:
A truss member is a two-force structural component connecting two joints. Its local response is governed by axial rigidity, length, and the extension projected along the member's axis.

In a two-dimensional model, direction cosines transform this local axial behavior into global x and y components. The sign of recovered axial stress distinguishes tension from compression.

Truss joint equilibrium requires the vector sum of member forces, applied loads, and reactions at a joint to vanish. Separate balance equations are written in the global coordinate directions.

Analytical joint equilibrium provides a useful check on a finite element solution. The assembled stiffness equations enforce the same balance through the nodal force and displacement relationships.

1265.title: Truss Element Stress Recovery
1265.heading: Truss Element Stress Recovery
1265.content:
Truss element stress recovery projects the global nodal displacement vector onto the member axis and divides the relative axial displacement by length. Multiplication by Young's modulus then yields normal stress.

The resulting scalar indicates the member's tensile or compressive state. It is computed after the unknown global nodal translations have been solved.

1268.title: Truss Element Stiffness Matrix
1268.heading: Truss Element Stiffness Matrix
1268.content:
A truss element stiffness matrix relates the four global translational degrees of freedom of a planar member to their nodal force components. Its scale is axial rigidity divided by length, and its pattern is built from direction-cosine products.

The matrix is symmetric and couples both nodes and both coordinate directions. Assembly adds each coefficient to the rows and columns associated with the element's global node numbers.

1271.title: Truss Direction Cosine
1271.heading: Truss Direction Cosine
1271.content:
A truss direction cosine is the cosine of the angle between a member axis and a global coordinate direction. In two dimensions, cosine and sine factors project local axial deformation and force into global x and y components.

These factors populate the oriented truss stiffness matrix. Reversing element orientation changes signed transformation terms while preserving the physical member response when node ordering is handled consistently.

1274.title: Truncation Error
1274.heading: Truncation Error
1274.content:
Truncation error arises when an infinite process is replaced by a finite one, such as stopping a series, derivative approximation, or iterative method after limited terms or steps.

It differs from [[Round-Off Error]], which comes from finite number representation. Increasing the number of terms reduces truncation error but may increase the amount of rounding accumulated.

1277.heading: True, Magnetic, and Compass Heading Conversion
1277.content: True track is measured from geographic north. Applying wind correction produces a true heading, applying magnetic variation converts it to magnetic heading, and applying compass deviation produces the heading to steer on that instrument. Keeping the stages separate prevents the direction reported by weather, the runway's magnetic label, and the compass indication from being mixed.

1280.title: Trophic Cascade
1280.heading: Trophic Cascade
1280.content:
A trophic cascade occurs when a change at one level of an ecology propagates through connected feeding and resource relationships to other levels. Removing or restoring a predator can indirectly change prey, vegetation, and the physical environment.

It demonstrates that effects can travel through several nested [[Feedback Loop|feedback loops]] rather than remain local to one pair of parts. This makes it a useful model for [[Game Ecology|game ecologies]] and other systemic simulations.
